title: Khadur Sahib
hook: where Guru Angad taught the script

segments.voice: Yesterday, Goindval and its baoli, walked slowly, one step at a time. Your line was step by step. What first step did you take? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

How did a child in Punjab learn to write before notebooks were cheap? On a wooden board, about the size of a schoolbook, smeared with a pale clay wash and left to dry in the sun. A child dips a reed pen in ink and writes letters on it, round and careful. When the board is full, it's washed clean, and the child starts again. Boards like this, called takhtis, are an old way of learning to write in Punjab. And Sikh tradition remembers a Guru who sat with children and their letters, in a small town near the Beas river: Khadur Sahib.
screen: `A WOODEN BOARD, A REED PEN.` → `WRITE, WASH, WRITE AGAIN.` → `KHADUR SAHIB.`

segments.voice: First, the Guru. Khadur was the town of Guru Angad, the second Guru, who took up the work after Guru Nanak. Tradition says he spent his days there among the sangat, and that he gave special care to teaching. Second, the script. Tradition says Guru Angad shaped and taught the letters now called Gurmukhi, and wrote out simple primers so children, and grown-ups too, could read the Guru's word for themselves. Gurmukhi is the script the Guru Granth Sahib is written in to this day. So when a Sikh child today learns to read Gurbani, the line of teaching runs back, in Sikh memory, to a teacher sitting with children here. Third, the alphabet as a teaching. Guru Nanak had already written a hymn on the letters, the Patti, in which, in paraphrase, each letter of the alphabet becomes a lesson about God and the self. Learning letters and learning the path were never two separate things. Fourth, the kitchen next door. The Guru Granth Sahib itself, in a ballad of the musicians Satta and Balwand, praises Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife. It says, in paraphrase, that she was a good woman whose shade was wide and leafy, and that in her langar, rice pudding with ghee was handed out to all. So Khadur Sahib holds both: a schoolroom and a kitchen. Letters for the mind, and food for anyone who came. Today the town keeps gurdwaras that remember Guru Angad, and children still learn their letters from the same alphabet.
screen: `GURU ANGAD AT KHADUR.` · `THE LETTERS OF GURMUKHI.` · `THE ALPHABET AS A LESSON.` · `MATA KHIVI'S KITCHEN.` · then, large: `WHERE THE SCRIPT GREW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a letter. Find a pen and a scrap of paper, or use your finger on your palm. Write one letter slowly: the first letter of your own name, or, if you'd like, the first letter of the Gurmukhi alphabet, called oora, which looks like a little curl with a tail. Write it once. Then again, slower. Breathe out as the pen moves. Notice the shape, the turn, the end of the stroke. Then rub it out, the way a child washes the board, and write it once more. The bell holds the time.
Khadur Sahib. The town of Guru Angad, where tradition says he taught the Gurmukhi letters, and where Mata Khivi's langar fed all who came. Today's word.
Your line: where the script grew. Today, write one thing by hand instead of typing it, a note, a list, a thank-you. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs visit Khadur Sahib to remember Guru Angad and Mata Khivi, and Sikh children learn to read Gurbani in the Gurmukhi script, often starting with the alphabet at a gurdwara Punjabi class.
